$comment: Category-level recommendation rules. These say what KINDS of product go with what, so the engine can then go and find whatever real, in-stock products exist — a rule naming products directly would have to be rewritten every time the catalogue changed. Product-specific pairings live on the product itself, under `relationships`.

max_recommendations.$comment: Section 54. Three is a suggestion; seventeen is a wall of upsell nobody reads.

accessory_budget_ratio.$comment: Default accessory spend as a fraction of the anchor's price. A 60k laptop justifies roughly 9k of accessories across all of them, which is why a 3k sleeve reads as reasonable and a 25k monitor does not.

max_accessory_price_ratio.$comment: An accessory costing more than the thing it accessorises is not an accessory. Hard exclusion, not a penalty — in a thin catalogue a merely-deprioritised candidate is still the top candidate.

upsell_max_uplift_ratio.$comment: An upsell may cost up to 25% more than the stated budget. Beyond that it stops being 'a bit more' and becomes ignoring what the customer said.

diversity.$comment: Section 51. Three results from one brand reads as a paid placement even when it is honestly ranked.

$comment_brand_ecosystems: Section 23. A brand match is a RANKING BOOST inside an already-relevant category, never a rule of its own — 'you bought Apple so here is Apple' is not a reason, but preferring AirPods among earbuds for an iPhone owner is.
